method: Incremental SCROLL-UNION walk of all 59 folder handles (mega-walk-union.ps1), then final-census.py with a mandatory self-check.

ROOT_CAUSE_OF_THE_13_2_GB_GAP.defect: THE MEGA GRID IS VIRTUALISED AND UN-MOUNTS ROWS YOU SCROLL PAST.
ROOT_CAUSE_OF_THE_13_2_GB_GAP.proof: Scrolling 2025-Feb to the BOTTOM REDUCED the visible row count from 36 to 31. A single before/after count measures a WINDOW, not a list.
ROOT_CAUSE_OF_THE_13_2_GB_GAP.correct_technique: Scroll in viewport-sized INCREMENTAL steps and UNION the rows visible at every position. Never jump to the end. Never count once.
ROOT_CAUSE_OF_THE_13_2_GB_GAP.SCOPE_OF_THE_DEFECT: EVERY count this project has ever taken measured a window — including the original census, whose own methodology note read 'row counts from this method are a lower bound until scrolling is proven.' It was never proven, and the note sat unactioned through four enumerations.

DEFINITIVE_FIGURES.actual_spend: NOT YET OBSERVED. Forecast and actual stay separate.

FIVE_CORRECTIONS_TO_THIS_CORPUS.note: Every correction has moved UPWARD. Each was found by reconciling a total against an independent figure, never by reading code.
FIVE_CORRECTIONS_TO_THIS_CORPUS.final_delta: 528.35 -> 630.74 is +19.4% on the original measurement, and +6.7% on the figure quoted to the operator most recently.
FIVE_CORRECTIONS_TO_THIS_CORPUS.why_it_matters: Every one of these would have been an UNDER-count, and under-counting a corpus means transcribing less of it than the operator paid for.

THE_2024_OVER_MEASUREMENT.observation: 2024 measures +3.51 GB against MEGA's own stated 107.41 GB for that year folder. You cannot measure more bytes than exist.
THE_2024_OVER_MEASUREMENT.hypothesis_tested: Double-counting — some folder in the 2024 tree appearing twice in the enumeration.
THE_2024_OVER_MEASUREMENT.test: Every title in all 14 of the 2024 month folders was checked against every other. Titles appearing in more than one folder: ZERO. Across the WHOLE share, exactly one title spans multiple folders: 'Resources Links.txt', a generic filename repeated across 4 bonus modules — not the same file.
THE_2024_OVER_MEASUREMENT.CONCLUSION: NOT double-counting. MEGA's stated year size (107.41 GB) is simply LOWER than the sum of its own stated month sizes. MEGA's displayed folder figures are NOT ADDITIVE.
THE_2024_OVER_MEASUREMENT.contradicts: The original census recorded that 'child sizes, names and counts all agree — the three independent drift dimensions'. For 2024 they do not agree.
THE_2024_OVER_MEASUREMENT.residual: 2022 -1.93 GB and 2023 -0.48 GB remain as sub-year shortfalls that offset the 2024 over. They sum with it to the 0.08 GB root-level residual, which is rounding.
THE_2024_OVER_MEASUREMENT.honest_reading: Per-folder stated figures cannot be used as an independent check. Only the ROOT total (319.95 GB) reconciles, and it does so to 0.025%.

TWO_MORE_DEFECTS_IN_THE_RECONCILIATION: PowerShell wraps a nested JSON array as {"value": [...], "Count": N}. Reading rows directly yields a dict, and iterating a dict yields its KEYS — producing a clean zero that reported 'folders failed: 0' and 'total files: 0' simultaneously.

A self-check was added that asserts the breakdown accounts for the same total as an independent tally, and prints *** MISMATCH *** and refuses to present the breakdown if it does not. Two earlier per-folder scripts lacked this and reported confident, wrong, few-GB totals.

WHAT_STILL_ITERATES.2022_and_2023_sub_year_shortfalls: 2022 -1.93 GB, 2023 -0.48 GB. NOT yet explained. They offset 2024's over at the root level, but individually they remain unexplained rather than reconciled.
WHAT_STILL_ITERATES.per_folder_stated_sizes: Unusable as a check — see the 2024 finding. Any future verification must compare against the ROOT total only.

NOT_MEASURED — DO NOT INFER: Whether the enumeration is now COMPLETE. The scroll-union is a strong method and the root total reconciles to 0.025%, but 'reconciles at the root' is weaker than 'every file was seen'. 656.90 h should still be treated as a near-floor, not a floor.
